subtopic: Theorem of Areas of Similar Triangles
stem: In \(\triangle ABC\), seg DE \(\parallel\) side BC. If \(2A(\triangle ADE) = A(\square DBCE)\), find \(AB : AD\) and show that \(BC = \sqrt{3}\, DE\).
solution: \(A(\square DBCE) = A(\triangle ABC) - A(\triangle ADE)\). Given \(2A(\triangle ADE) = A(\square DBCE) = A(\triangle ABC) - A(\triangle ADE)\), so \(3A(\triangle ADE) = A(\triangle ABC)\), i.e. \(\dfrac{A(\triangle ADE)}{A(\triangle ABC)} = \dfrac{1}{3}\). Since DE \(\parallel\) BC, \(\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC\), and the ratio of areas equals the ratio of squares of corresponding sides: \(\dfrac{AD^2}{AB^2} = \dfrac{DE^2}{BC^2} = \dfrac{1}{3}\). \(\therefore \dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), so \(AB : AD = \sqrt{3} : 1\). Also \(\dfrac{DE}{BC} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), hence \(BC = \sqrt{3}\, DE\).

stem: \(\triangle SHR \sim \triangle SVU\). In \(\triangle SHR\), \(SH = 4.5\) cm, \(HR = 5.2\) cm, \(SR = 5.8\) cm and \(\dfrac{SH}{SV} = \dfrac{3}{5}\). Construct \(\triangle SVU\).
solution: Since \(\dfrac{SH}{SV} = \dfrac{3}{5}\), we have \(\dfrac{SV}{SH} = \dfrac{5}{3}\), so \(\triangle SVU\) is larger than \(\triangle SHR\) with scale factor \(\dfrac{5}{3}\). Steps: (1) Construct \(\triangle SHR\) with \(SH = 4.5\) cm, \(HR = 5.2\) cm, \(SR = 5.8\) cm. (2) Draw ray SB making an acute angle with side SR, on the side opposite to H. (3) Mark 5 equal points \(S_1, S_2, S_3, S_4, S_5\) on ray SB. (4) Join \(S_3 R\). Through \(S_5\) draw a line parallel to \(S_3 R\) meeting ray SR (extended) at U. (5) Through U draw a line parallel to HR meeting ray SH (extended) at V. Then \(\triangle SVU\) is the required triangle similar to \(\triangle SHR\) with \(\dfrac{SV}{SH} = \dfrac{5}{3}\).

subtopic: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
stem: An ice-cream pot has a right circular cylindrical shape. The radius of the base is 12 cm and the height is 7 cm. This pot is completely filled with ice-cream. The entire ice-cream is given to students in the form of right circular ice-cream cones having diameter 4 cm and height 3.5 cm. If each student is given one cone, how many students can be served?
solution: Volume of the cylindrical pot \(= \pi r^2 h = \pi \times 12^2 \times 7 = 1008\pi\) cubic cm. For each cone, radius \(= \dfrac{4}{2} = 2\) cm and height \(= 3.5\) cm, so volume of one cone \(= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi \times 2^2 \times 3.5 = \dfrac{14\pi}{3}\) cubic cm. Number of students \(= \dfrac{\text{volume of pot}}{\text{volume of one cone}} = \dfrac{1008\pi}{\frac{14\pi}{3}} = \dfrac{1008 \times 3}{14} = 216\). Hence 216 students can be served.
